newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Debt supply under EMU to challenge U.S.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Debt supply under EMU to challenge U.S.

text.p: The new euro bond market has the potential to challenge U.S. Treasuries in size and depth, far outstripping the current outstanding Ecu bonds, analysts said.

Details as to how supply will be issued, what the yield curve will look like and where supply will be weighted have yet to emerge. Much will depend on which countries qualify for entry into European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"It is an absolutely awesome number, which creates the second biggest market in (the) world, bigger than Japan," said Steve Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais in Paris.

He estimated the total amount of government debt in Europe would be around 70 to 75 percent of the size of the U.S. Treasuries market, which is currently around $3.5 trillion, whereas the Ecu bond market totals around $130 billion.
"European total debt of around $2.0 trillion would need to be issued, which makes the Ecu bond market just a drop in the ocean," Major said.

Graham Bishop, EU advisor at Salomon Brothers International in London, said the total number of bonds in the euro would be about the same size or slightly larger than the U.S. Treasury market, based on the Salomon's world index of government bonds.
"That will be the tradeable universe for clients and there's no particular reason to expect it to change dramatically," said Bishop.
But Werner Becker, senior economist at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt said the need to cover all areas of the curve would inevitably lead to an increase in the number of debt products.

"EMU will lead to a greater variety of debt instruments for government debt. Availablity of all instruments on all points of the yield curve will be crucial. There will be fierce competition between the various issuers," he said.
"The volume of single bonds and notes will be much bigger than now because the most liquid instruments will become benchmarks, and benchmarking means lower costs for governments."
Major said Germany would provide the benchmarks with Germany and France being the biggest issuers of new paper, with Belgium also a leading player once existing debt was converted.
"The credit spreads and main liquidity will be in the markets of Germany and France," he said.

Major said the question of how much relevance the credit guarantee, supposedly implicit in the EU, would have behind the debt was still being worked out. "It's more or less one bond market with a bit of credit and liquidity spread," he said.
Major said the conversion of existing debt, would create some secondary market trading along with the refinancing of maturing debt that had been rolled over.

"There will be a big pool of tradeable bonds pretty quickly because of the early changeover," he said. "Countries like France and Belgium have been keen to state that they are to have their paper denominated in euros from January 1999."
Decisions about maturities and sizes of issues will probably be made at a national level, analysts said.

Stephen King, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London, said in the short term there would be nothing to prevent countries borrowing as much as they wanted. "The restraint will be via the stability pact when it is up and running," King said.
He likened it to local authorities or individual states in the U.S. issuing paper and theoretically, being free to issue as much as they wanted.
Credit Lyonnais' Major said the pact would probably be more important than the Maastricht deficit criteria of three percent and would provide a shrinking basis for debt.

"The three-percent target can be hit by anyone on a cosmetic basis, but what is important to financal markets and longer-term credibility is a sustainable reduction in the deficit. and that is what the German plan would enforce," he said.
Bishop said the size of the relative weighting was already determined for many years by the existing stock of bonds in participating countries and by the new deficits which they have.
He said under EMU a government would no longer have to worry about currency because it would be part of the euro bloc.
"At the moment, if a government borrows too much, the risk is either interest rates have to rise quite quickly or the exchange rate starts to suffer, or possibly a combination of both," he said.

"The incentive to become a fiscal free rider is much greater because you can borrow more, and there is no exchange rate risk associated with that," he said. "The problem would be if everyone decided to do that at the same time a huge deficit would build up. Hence the stability pact."
Analysts were undecided about which auctioning technique would be adopted by countries participating in EMU.
Becker said there were currently three auctioning systems, a primary dealer system, tenders and consortium proceedures.
He said the consortium procedure was not particularly profitable or efficient, so he expected to see a primary dealer system and a tender procedure in nearly all national markets.

Bishop said it was too early to tell what system would be adopted and that it would probably be an evolutionary process as countries found the most efficient system with the minimimum yield spreads in order to reduce government costs.
"Each country will do its own thing as they always have. There will be no currency question. It will simply be what is the credit quality, and that is measured in basis points of yield," Bishop said.
But he said for now the French approach was being widely adopted world wide. Major agreed saying the French OAT market would be the system to copy.

"In European government bond markets, the role model of how to create transparency and liquidity has been created by the French. The only other country that is as good as France is Spain because they have literally copied the French system and Portugal is going the same way," he said.
